C: Keep a documented safety and quality system (paper or electronic) that covers the CSQ requirements, names the people and backups who maintain it, holds every SOP, program, form, log, diagram and training material plus local regulations, is available to staff, sets the rules for using the CSQ logo, and is kept up to date.
Hendrix is the electronic system; Rulebook holds each state's regulations; logs and records. SOP library: every SOP, numbered, versioned, approved and signed.

Have a written safety, quality and compliance policy with measurable objectives, shared with staff, backed by resources, that keeps staff informed of new science and regulation and is reviewed regularly.

Write the safety, quality and compliance policy as an SOP; everyone signs it. Quality policy (signed SOP) linked on Quality Objectives, with measurable objectives, owners and targets. Management review checks the policy and objectives at least yearly.
Procedures that keep all operations and products compliant where they are made and sold, with compliance staff trained and current on regulations.
Rulebook per state; licenses per state. Regulatory training tracked per person.

Control documents and records: a master list, document type and current version, approved changes and replacement of old versions, legible and available records, secure storage for at least 1 year past the date on the label (or longer if required), ink only and no white-out on paper.

Audit trail: every change kept with who, when and why; records are voided, never deleted. SOP library: master list, document numbers, versions, approval by Full access, every earlier version kept unchanged, review dates; audit trail on every record.

Audit every applicable CSQ requirement at least once a year with competent auditors who do not audit their own work; record findings and corrective actions, share results, and close findings through CAPA.

Internal Audits: annual program of every CSQ clause in scope with coverage shown per clause, auditor named with qualification and confirmed independent, checklist results with evidence, a finding for every nonconformity, findings closed through deviations / CAPA with verification, results shared with staff before closing.

Document every deviation and nonconformance clearly with root cause (when an authorized person decides one is needed), owner, immediate correction, timescale, effectiveness check, and review the trend at least once a year.
QMS: numbered deviations with correction, authorized root-cause decision, owner and due date; CAPAs closed only when verified effective; monthly trends and a printable annual review.
Name who investigates and resolves complaints, track and analyze complaint data, and record the corrective actions taken to stop them happening again.

Complaints: numbered, named investigator and due date, investigation, root cause, resolution, corrective action and linked deviation / CAPA, response to the complainant, adverse events reported to the regulator, trends by month, category, lot and customer.

Recall and withdrawal procedures that meet regulation: a recall team with roles, an up-to-date contact list (team, emergency services, customers, suppliers, regulators, certification body), a communication plan, recovery or disposal of product, and a yearly mock recall completed in under 2 hours.

Batch numbers and final package tags. Shipments show which customers received each batch; recalled product goes on hold. Traceability and Recall: recall team with roles and backups, contact list (emergency, regulators, certification body, customers, suppliers, lab) verified yearly, timed mock recalls (server clock, pass only if every step is done within 2 hours), real recalls and withdrawals that put affected product on hold and record who was notified and when.

Protect against theft, bioterrorism and intentional adulteration: threat assessment, access to sensitive areas limited to authorized people, cannabis materials, waste and product secured, secure transport, training for security and transport staff, and a yearly review and test.

Visitor Log and kiosk; security malfunction and security inspection logs; role-based access in Hendrix. Product defense training tracked per person. Risk register: threat assessment (product defense) with owner, controls and yearly review. Photo badges with a secret QR / barcode (re-issued when lost) and a badge time clock per license: only people with access to the license can clock in; who is on site is known at any time (roll call).
Assess vulnerability to mislabeling, substitution, dilution and counterfeiting, control what is found, verify label claims (strain, cannabinoid content and similar), and review and test yearly.
Sticker potency is taken from the COA; COA tag mismatches are flagged. Risk register: fraud vulnerability assessment (substitution, dilution, mislabeling, counterfeiting) reviewed yearly.

Crisis procedures with the people responsible and their contacts, emergency contacts, response to foreseeable disasters, how affected product is found, isolated and released, how authorities and customers are told, and a yearly review and test.
Crisis plan kept as an SOP. Recall team and emergency contacts; affected product found with the trace and isolated with holds.

Buildings, grounds and utilities suit their purpose and prevent cross-contamination: cleanable surfaces in good repair, enough and protected lighting, shatterproof or protected glass, ventilation, sealed and screened openings, handwash stations at production entries (potable warm water, hands-free soap, paper towels), plumbing and wastewater that work, restrooms, changing and break areas sized for the shift, required signage, and clear aisles.

Keep buildings, grounds and amenities in good repair and clean: no debris, standing water or excessive dust, vegetation managed against pests, restrooms and break areas stocked and sanitary, roadways and docks clear.
Sanitation Log (weekly and monthly areas); Equipment Maintenance Log.

Equipment and utensils suit their purpose, are installed to regulation, cleanable and kept in repair, stored safely, have approved controls, hoses on racks off the floor, and measuring instruments that are accurate and maintained.

Equipment register: every piece of equipment with location, serial, product contact and critical flags, controls and who approved them; master preventive maintenance schedule with manufacturer tasks (work recorded in the Equipment Maintenance Log); temporary repairs with a fix-by date until made permanent; out of service and back in service with tools / debris removed, cleaned and test run.

Maintenance procedures with a master preventive maintenance schedule (including manufacturer requirements), records of unplanned work, a way for staff to report repairs that threaten product, no contamination left after maintenance, and control of temporary repairs so they do not become permanent.

Equipment Maintenance Log records work done. Repairs that threaten product are reported as deviations from the maintenance log. Equipment register: every piece of equipment with location, serial, product contact and critical flags, controls and who approved them; master preventive maintenance schedule with manufacturer tasks (work recorded in the Equipment Maintenance Log); temporary repairs with a fix-by date until made permanent; out of service and back in service with tools / debris removed, cleaned and test run.

Every instrument that affects safety or quality is listed and identified with a valid calibration certificate and due date, calibrated on time by recognized methods, with weights traceable to a reference standard (NIST, ASTM), and protected from damage or adjustment.

Scale Calibration Log. Equipment register: instruments that need calibration with interval, method, reference standard (NIST / ASTM) and protection from adjustment; each calibration with its certificate and next due date; a failed calibration takes the instrument out of service.

Cleaning procedures say what is cleaned, how and with which chemicals, how often (by risk), who cleans and who verifies; tools are color-coded or labeled, clean and dirty tools are stored apart, and cleaning never puts product at risk.

Sanitation Log: daily, weekly and monthly areas, equipment, chemical and concentration, and a second person who verifies the cleaning (visual, ATP swab or checklist). Facility Tests: food-contact surface swabs (ATP / micro) verify cleaning.

Identify, separate and dispose of every waste type to regulation: waste areas and containers labeled, cleaned, emptied regularly, closed, restricted when required, and wastewater treated when required.
Waste Destruction Log: categories, 4 camera angles, rendering and disposal locations, methods.
Cannabinoid waste is never mixed with other waste streams.
Each non-cannabinoid waste stream (municipal, hazardous, recyclables) is kept separate.

Risk-based pest program reviewed yearly: responsibilities, an accurate trap and bait station map, stations placed safely, approved pesticides with SDS, monitoring frequency, sightings recorded and trended, contractor recommendations acted on, rules for touching trap contents, pesticide use and storage to label and law, and cleanup of exposed areas and product.

Pest Control Log: numbered trap and bait stations checked on every visit, stations with activity, sightings counted, treatments and vendor license. Attach the station map here. Pest sightings can be raised as deviations from the log. Chemicals and SDS: pesticides approved with SDS and EPA registration number.
Pest control staff and contractors are trained, licensed when required, use only approved products, and leave a written report of findings and products used.
Pest control contractor approved in Suppliers with applicator license on file.
Air entering production areas is filtered and monitored by risk, tested at least yearly by an ISO/IEC 17025 lab, and air handling controls contaminants, fumes and odors.
Temp / Humidity Log. Facility Tests: air tested on schedule (at least yearly) by an ISO/IEC 17025 lab, with limits, reports and corrective actions.

Water is potable, filtered and monitored by risk, tested at least yearly by an ISO/IEC 17025 lab, tempered for washing, treated water meets spec, backflow devices are fitted and tested yearly, and the water system is monitored.

Equipment register: water treatment and HVAC equipment with maintenance schedules. Facility Tests: incoming and process water tested at least yearly by an ISO/IEC 17025 lab; backflow devices tested yearly.
Environmental monitoring program: who runs it and their competence, a risk assessment of hazards per area, sampling methods, frequency and limits, recording and trending, and a yearly review.
Dry goods stored in identified, suitable areas, off the floor and away from walls, and not mixed.

Chemical approval process and approved list, SDS on file for every chemical, storage to SDS and label, food-grade kept apart from non-food-grade, original or labeled containers, ventilated and restricted storage with PPE, first aid, spill kits and a chemical list, and disposal to regulation.

Chemicals and SDS: approved chemical list (approval by Full access), SDS required before approval, food grade kept apart from non-food grade, storage area, restricted access, hazards, PPE, first aid, spill response and disposal; printable chemical list for every storage area.

Goods needing temperature or atmosphere control have defined specs; storage areas are identified, clean, working and fitted with monitoring devices; cold and frozen units have thermometers; goods off the floor and not mixed; condensation drains away from product.
Temp / Humidity Log: min and max per room; out-of-range readings are marked automatically and need a corrective action. Out-of-range readings can be raised as deviations from the log.
Loading and unloading limit damage: inspection before loading or unloading, minimal exposure, no cross-contamination, goods secured from tampering, and cannabis shipped and received to regulation.
Receiving inspection (vehicle, packaging, seals) and pre-load inspection that must pass before shipping.

Every inventory item is identified through the process, finished product is traceable one step forward to the customer, materials and supplies one step back to the supplier, traceability is kept through rework, and it is tested at least yearly in a mock recall.

Batch numbers, final package tags, state tracking system (METRC). Lots numbered on receipt and linked to the batches that use them (one step back); shipments list batches and package tags per customer (one step forward). Trace any lot, batch or package tag one step back and one step forward; traceability tested by the yearly mock recall.

Incoming materials meet specs, are inspected for damage, arrive with a COA or certificate of conformance, are sampled and tested when needed, have their documents reviewed before approval or rejection, and rejected goods are returned or held apart.

Approved supplier list and COA expiry in Suppliers. Receiving: lots only from approved suppliers, inspected on arrival, COA required, quarantined until accepted or rejected by Full access; rejected lots held apart automatically.

FIFO (or similar) rotation for finished product, WIP, rework and supplies; nothing used past its date; overflow storage monitored; labels, packaging, devices and excise stamps counted in an inventory system and protected from theft.
Inventory by lot: quantity left, expiry, oldest-first (FIFO) prompt; expired or held lots cannot be used.

Nonconforming and returned goods are clearly marked, quarantined so they cannot be released by accident, decided on only by qualified authorized people, and released, moved or destroyed to regulation.

Testing status (Pending, Failed, Retest); final results changed only with Full access and a reason. Nonconforming product recorded as a deviation (from a failed test or batch) with the decision documented. Hold and Release: lots, batches, package tags and customer returns put on hold by anyone with Edit; only Full access decides (release, destroy, return, rework) with a reason; held items cannot be used or shipped.

Name each supplier and vendor type and the specs they must meet, verify them, select, approve and monitor them, keep an approved list, name who approves, allow emergency suppliers with checks, require ethical sourcing, audit contract manufacturers, and review all suppliers yearly.

Approved supplier list per license: supplier type, specs, credentials with expiry, who approved and on what basis, emergency suppliers with verification, ethical sourcing, contract manufacturer audits, yearly reviews (6 months for high risk), suspend and disqualify with reasons.
Documented SOPs for producing and processing cannabinoid materials and products that conform to CSQ and regulation.
Batch Tracker records follow each process. SOP library for every production process; Batch Tracker records follow them.
Document how people and product move through the facility to keep segregation, with a map of area designations and their risks.
Process flow and area map attached to an SOP.
Before production, record a check that areas and equipment are clean, within maintenance and calibration dates and ready, with any problem and correction noted.

Line Clearance: a pre-operational inspection before each batch (previous product and labels removed, cleaned, equipment in date, materials staged, cGMP dress, no foreign matter, tools counted); every problem recorded with its correction; the line cannot be cleared with uncorrected failures or with equipment out of service or out of calibration.

Every material and supply has specs and is identified by type, use and hazard; meets regulation and is approved for use; is fit for purpose; has a yearly risk assessment; label information is kept on file; and is stored and used to label instructions.

Products: ingredient price library and formulations. Material specs required of each supplier; only approved suppliers used. Materials received with specs, COA and inspection; used only after acceptance. Risk register: materials and suppliers risk assessment, reviewed yearly.
Rework is identified and dated for traceability, each batch inspected and analyzed before use, used before it would expire in the finished product, safe, and like-to-like.

Rework: numbered, dated and tagged; source batch or hold; inspected and analyzed before release; approved by Full access as like-to-like; cannot be used in a product that expires after the rework; used in a traceable batch or destroyed with a reason.

Keep foreign matter out: exclude contamination sources, no loose objects overhead, inspection of facility and tools, a list of sources that cannot be removed with protective measures, control of blades, glass and brittle items, dust and chemicals, cleanup and release of contaminated areas, decisions on affected product, detection and removal methods, investigation, and calibrated detection equipment.
Contamination incidents reported as deviations with correction and root cause.
Allergen labeling meets the law, allergen labels are verified, allergens from materials, suppliers, staff and visitors are risk-assessed, and cleaning, changeover and storage prevent cross-contact.
Label templates carry an allergen declaration that prints on every sticker. Risk register: allergen risk assessment of materials, suppliers, staff and visitors.

Label specs that meet CSQ and regulation; label content (potency, ingredients, allergens, warnings, claims, batch) verified against the batch; labels reviewed when materials, processes or rules change; only the labels and packaging a batch needs are issued, then reconciled; no mislabeled or damaged product; correct, inspected, clean packaging materials and tools.
Sticker templates per SKU and flavor with approval number; potency printed from the COA; every sticker print logged (batch, tag, count, who); template changes in the audit trail.

Finished product meets spec and regulation before release; samples are representative; samplers are competent; methods, frequency and limits are defined and results trended; held product is released after review; recognized methods; compliance labs accredited to ISO/IEC 17025; internal labs separated; retention samples kept when required.

Testing: per final package tag, lab and lab license, COA stored privately, COA read by AI with tag check, retention samples (quantity, location, keep-until). Testing labs approved in Suppliers with ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation; labs used in Testing are checked against the approved list. Batches with a failed test and no passing retest cannot be released from hold or shipped.
Everyone in the facility is classified by role; each role has defined duties and requirements (certifications, education, experience, training).
Roles with duties, requirements (certifications, training, experience) and access per person. Each role's required training in the training matrix.

Train everyone, including temps and contractors, before they work: minimum training for all, training per role, a training matrix, yearly refreshers, regular assessments, legal, cGMP (cultivation also current Good Agricultural and Collection Practices, cGACP), cannabis safety, hygiene, product defense and job training; at least one person with CSQ program overview training; qualified trainers; training in a language staff understand; records kept at least for the length of employment.

Roles (the training matrix will hang off them). SOP signatures per person are part of the training record. Training matrix: required courses by role, refreshers, qualified trainers, assessments, certificates, SOP signatures; CSQ Program Overview holders counted.

Staff know the symptoms that keep them off product and how to report them; no handling product with open wounds; minor cuts covered with bandage and glove; bodily fluid spills quarantined, cleaned and released by authorized people.

Staff come to work clean; no false nails, nail polish or false eyelashes; no heavy perfume; eating, drinking and smoking only in permitted areas; protect product from sweat and skin medicines; smokers wash hands on return; hair can be contained.
GMP hygiene SOP signed by everyone. Hygiene training tracked per person.
No jewelry except a plain band or medical bracelet; jewelry that cannot come off is covered; suitable outer garments; loose items removed and long hair tied back; storage for personal items.
GMP clothing and jewelry SOP signed by everyone. Hygiene training tracked per person.

PPE defined by risk assessment for each task and available to staff and visitors, replaced and cleaned as needed, clean and dirty PPE kept apart, and hair nets, beard nets and gloves worn wherever product is exposed.
PPE SOP signed by everyone. PPE training tracked per person.

Staff are trained and wash at the right times (after contamination risks, when soiled, when changing gloves, after breaks, eating, smoking or the restroom); stations are accessible with handwash signs in a language staff understand.
QR sign printing for posted signs. Handwashing SOP signed by everyone. Handwashing training tracked per person.

Visitors and contractors stay out of production when ill, acknowledge the facility's cGMP rules, wear suitable clothing and PPE, remove jewelry and loose items, and follow hygiene and handwashing rules.
Visitor Log and QR kiosk: every visitor reads and accepts the GMP rules and answers an illness question before entering; anyone ill is marked to stay out of production.

Indoor grows follow cGACP and protect plants from disease, pests, foreign matter and microbes: areas identified with signage; air quality specs; air conditioned, filtered, treated and monitored; air handling checked; airflow, humidity and temperature with min and max limits and no stagnant air.
Temp / Humidity Log with min and max per room. Facility Tests: grow room air quality tested on schedule. Cultivation: indoor grow areas with temperature, humidity and airflow limits.

Outdoor sites are documented (area, intended use) and registered; the site and neighboring land are risk-assessed (land use history, topography, controls) and re-evaluated yearly; animals kept out of fields and water; handwashing and toilets (or other hygiene means) provided.

Cultivation: outdoor fields with land use history and a site risk assessment re-evaluated yearly. Risk register: site and neighboring land risks (land use history, drift, flooding, water) reviewed yearly.
Greenhouses apply the indoor and outdoor cultivation requirements that fit them.
Cultivation: greenhouses recorded as grow areas with their risk assessment.

Cultivation equipment and utensils are easy to clean and repair, identified for their use (color coded or labeled), stored apart from materials and product, hoses emptied and on racks off the floor, and field and transport vehicles clean and in good repair.
Equipment Maintenance Log. Equipment register: cultivation equipment and vehicles with maintenance schedules.
Every cultivation input is declared with safety and quality specs, and its use is controlled, recorded and tracked.
Inputs from approved suppliers received as numbered lots with COA. Cultivation: every nutrient, amendment and crop protection product applied per plant batch, from approved inputs or accepted lots.
Air, CO2 and other process gases

Gases used in the grow and in processing suit their use and their levels are monitored: filtered, dry and oil-free; at least 99.5% pure unless specified; CO2 beverage grade or better (never medical grade).
Gas suppliers approved with specs; gases received with COA.
Growth additives, fertilizers, nutrients and soil amendments

An integrated nutrient management plan: approved list and who approves, inputs identified and stored away from water, use guided by sample analysis, organic where possible, organic and inorganic stored apart, no untreated manure, untreated amendments treated and verified.
Approved nutrient suppliers and received lots; the nutrient plan as an SOP. Cultivation: approved inputs (Chemicals and SDS) form the nutrient plan; every application recorded with rate and method.
Grow media are evaluated for hazards, never used untreated, and reused media are treated and verified against specs.
Grow media received as lots with specs. Cultivation: grow media lot and treatment recorded per plant batch.

Soil meets food crop requirements: characteristics known and evaluated as a contamination source, sampled and tested on a continuing basis, informed by past tests and land use, with erosion monitored.
Facility Tests: soil / grow media sampled and tested on a continuing basis.
Irrigation water meets food crop requirements, is evaluated as a contamination source, tested on a continuing basis, informed by past tests and land use, with wastewater monitored.
Facility Tests: irrigation water and wastewater tested on a continuing basis.

Ice meets the water specs; ice machines installed to regulation with storage and production parts emptied and cleaned at least weekly; dry ice used sparingly, only for temperature, never touching product.
Processes using ice or dry ice

Water sources and system type identified; systems designed and installed safely with no lead pipes or fittings; tested for contaminants at a set frequency; maintained to avoid waste and wet media that grows mold; applied to plant needs without runoff; water use measured with reduction, retention and reclamation where possible.
Equipment Maintenance Log. Facility Tests: irrigation water tested for contaminants at a set frequency. Cultivation: irrigation / fertigation system and water source recorded per area.
Cuttings, clones, seeds and propagation materials

Propagation material comes from licensed or approved sources (with specs and acceptance) or own plants, is kept healthy and from becoming a contamination source, is labeled with name, source, date and other details, and retention samples are kept when required.

Clone and seed suppliers approved; propagation material received as lots. Cultivation: plant batches traced to the received clone / seed lot or own mother; printable labels with name, source and date.
Crop maintenance and protection follow each plant's growth and the plant part to be used.
Pest Control Log. Cultivation: crop protection with approved pesticides (EPA number, rate, applicator, REI, PHI) and scouting records; harvest is blocked until the pre-harvest interval ends.
Harvest protects fresh material from foreign matter and microbes: cGACP in the field, cGMP once indoors.
Cultivation: harvest with wet weight and METRC harvest tag.
Drying, curing and other post-harvest work follow cGMP and protect material from foreign matter and microbes.
Temp / Humidity Log for dry and cure rooms. Cultivation: drying and curing with room conditions and final dry weight.
Grinding and milling follow cGMP; areas are monitored for dust and have dust handling and PPE.
Tissue culture follows cGMP and protects cultures from foreign matter and microbes.

Defined procedures and equipment; materials measured and added at the right step; parameters documented to spec; homogeneous batches; rework approved by qualified staff; equipment sized for the batch.
Live products such as seeds are protected from foreign matter, chemical and microbial contamination.
Dried or fresh frozen flower is protected from foreign matter, chemical and microbial contamination, kept frozen when required, and handled with airflow, ventilation and dust control.
Lab results per batch in Testing; storage conditions in the Temp / Humidity Log.
Pre-rolls are protected from foreign matter, chemical and microbial contamination, with airflow, ventilation and dust control where they are made.
Pre-rolls made at a cultivation license

Extraction and refinement follow cGMP and protect product from adulterants, foreign matter and residual solvents: areas identified with signage, simultaneous activities segregated, spill kits next to every extraction area, closed-loop systems where applicable built to the safety standards for their use, equipment cleanable in place, and solvent and chemical levels in the final product within regulation and spec.
Ethanol and BHO extraction batch records; residual solvent results on COAs. Equipment register: extraction systems with maintenance, calibration and validation.

Solvent extraction is done by trained, competent staff: fire and life safety systems working and within maintenance and calibration before use; areas and equipment designed for the solvent used; cleaning suited to the solvent and its residues.

Ethanol and BHO batch records; Equipment Maintenance Log; training per person. Equipment register: gas detection and fire safety systems kept within maintenance and calibration; out-of-date equipment cannot be put back in service. Line Clearance for extraction batches adds gas detection, fire and life safety, ventilation and solvent checks.

Solventless work (ice water, dry sift, rosin) is done by trained staff in separate areas: enough drainage, process water at least potable and to spec before use, water removed from the product to spec and from waste before disposal, equipment fit to carry that water, defined environmental conditions (walk-in coolers and freezers included).
Temp / Humidity Log for the rooms used. Facility Tests: process water and ice tested to spec.
Every extraction and refinement input is declared with safety and quality specs, and its use is controlled, recorded and tracked.
Inputs from approved suppliers, received as numbered lots with COA and recorded against the extraction batches that use them.
Air, CO2, LPG and other process gases

Process gases (air, CO2, butane, propane, nitrogen...) suit their use and their levels are monitored in the area, on the person, in the process and in the product: filtered, dry and oil-free; at least 99.5% pure unless specified; CO2 beverage grade or better (never medical grade).
Gas suppliers approved with specs (purity, beverage grade CO2); gases received with COA / certificate of conformance. Facility Tests: process gases tested / COA per delivery for purity.
Ethanol and other liquid organic solvents

Solvents suit their use and their levels are monitored: at least 99.5% pure; ethanol food grade and not denatured (approved denaturants reduced to legal levels if used); only ethanol may be an ingredient, and then it must be food grade and not denatured.
Ethanol batch records track solvent use; solvents from approved suppliers received with COA.
Water used during extraction and refinement
Process water is potable and at least 99.5% pure, evaluated as a contamination source, tested on a continuing basis, informed by past tests and land use, with wastewater monitored.
Facility Tests: process water and wastewater tested on a continuing basis.

Ice meets the water specs; ice machines installed to regulation with storage and production parts emptied and cleaned at least weekly; dry ice used sparingly, only for temperature, and never touching product.
Other solid and liquid processing inputs

Media, chemicals, catalysts and reactants are at least 99.5% pure and food grade, or justified by a toxicological risk assessment; non-food-grade inputs are declared and reduced to safe levels in the final product.
Processing input suppliers approved with specs; inputs received with COA.
Terpenes and other ingredients added to extracts are food grade or justified by a toxicological risk assessment; non-food-grade ingredients are declared and reduced to safe levels.
Formulations list ingredients; ingredient suppliers approved with specs; ingredients received with COA.
Indoor air quality, airflow and environment

Extraction and processing areas have air quality specs; air is conditioned, filtered, treated and monitored; air handling is checked; airflow, humidity and temperature have min and max limits and air never stagnates; milling and grinding areas are monitored for dust with dust handling and PPE.
Temp / Humidity Log: min and max per room; out-of-range readings need a corrective action. Facility Tests: extraction area air quality tested on schedule.

Defined procedures and equipment for blending; every ingredient measured and added at the right step; parameters documented to spec; batches homogeneous before dispensing; rework approved by qualified staff; equipment sized for the batch.
Formulations; Batch Tracker calculations; changes to filled values need Full access and a reason. Rework to bring a batch into specification is approved by Full access (qualified person) before use.
Dried or fresh frozen biomass is protected from foreign matter, chemical and microbial contamination, kept frozen until use when required, and handled with airflow, ventilation and dust control.
Biomass received as numbered lots; storage conditions in the Temp / Humidity Log.
Concentrates and extracts are protected from contamination; residual solvents (also in solventless products) stay within the stricter of regulation or internal spec.
Testing stores residual solvent results from COAs; a failed result puts the batch on hold.
Cannabinoids made by conversion, synthesis or modified organisms are declared, have safety and quality specs, and their use is controlled, recorded and tracked.
Batch records and formulations record what is made and used.

Formulated substances are protected from contamination, risk-assessed for route of administration and labeled with it, carry allergen declarations when used as ingredients, and use inhalation-grade ingredients when meant for inhalation (food grade or GRAS alone is not enough).
SKU specs and formulations; inhalable ingredient suppliers approved with an inhalation-grade statement.

Manufacturing follows cGMP and protects product from adulterants, foreign matter and residual solvents: areas identified with signage, simultaneous activities segregated, solvent and chemical levels in the final product within regulation and spec.
Batch records; residual solvent results on COAs.
Every manufacturing input is declared with safety and quality specs, and its use is controlled, recorded and tracked.
Formulations; batch records capture inputs used. Inputs received as numbered lots and recorded against the batches that use them.
Air, CO2 and other process gases
Process gases suit their use and are monitored: filtered, dry and oil-free; at least 99.5% pure unless specified; CO2 beverage grade or better (never medical grade).
Gas suppliers approved with specs (purity, beverage grade CO2). Gases received with COA / certificate of conformance.
Ethanol and other liquid organic solvents

Solvents suit their use and are monitored: at least 99.5% pure; ethanol food grade and not denatured (approved denaturants reduced to legal levels if used); only ethanol may be an ingredient, and it must be food grade.
Ethanol and BHO batch records track solvent use. Solvents received with COA / certificate of conformance.

Water used as an ingredient or in processing is potable, at least 99.5% pure, evaluated as a contamination source, tested on a continuing basis, informed by past tests and land use, with wastewater monitored.
Facility Tests: water used in manufacturing and wastewater tested on a continuing basis.
Ice meets water specs; ice machines installed to regulation with storage and production parts emptied and cleaned at least weekly; dry ice used sparingly and never touching product.
Processes using ice or dry ice
Other solid and liquid processing inputs

Media, catalysts, reactants and similar inputs are at least 99.5% pure and food grade, or justified by a toxicological risk assessment; non-food-grade inputs are declared and reduced to safe levels in the final product.
Processing input suppliers approved with specs. Processing inputs received with COA.
Terpenes and other ingredients are food grade or justified by a toxicological risk assessment; non-food-grade ingredients are declared and reduced to safe levels.
Formulations list ingredients. Ingredient suppliers approved with specs (food grade, COA). Ingredients received with COA and inspection.
Indoor air quality, airflow and environment

Production areas have air quality specs; air is conditioned, filtered, treated and monitored; air handling is checked; airflow, humidity and temperature have min and max limits and air never stagnates; milling and grinding areas are monitored for dust with dust handling and PPE.
Temp / Humidity Log: min and max per room; out-of-range readings are marked automatically and need a corrective action.

Defined procedures and equipment for blending; every ingredient measured and added at the right step; parameters documented to spec; batches homogeneous before dispensing; rework approved by qualified staff; equipment sized for the batch.
Formulations; Batch Tracker calculations; changes to filled values need Full access and a reason.
Dried or frozen flower is protected from foreign matter, chemical and microbial contamination, kept frozen when required, and handled with airflow, ventilation and dust control.
Infused flower, moon rocks and snow caps batch records.
Pre-rolls are protected from contamination with dust control; ingredients for infused pre-rolls are fit for inhalation (food grade or GRAS alone is not enough).
Pre-roll batch type with coating (Kief, Diamond). Infusion ingredient suppliers approved with an inhalation-grade statement.

Concentrates and extracts are protected from contamination; residual solvents (also in solventless products) stay within the stricter of regulation or internal spec; converted or synthetic cannabinoids are declared, specified and tracked.
Testing stores residual solvent results from COAs.

Formulated substances are protected from contamination, risk-assessed for route of administration and labeled with it, carry allergen declarations when used as ingredients, and use inhalation-grade ingredients when meant for inhalation.
Inhalable products are protected from contamination, risk-assessed for inhalation, and use only ingredients fit for inhalation (food grade or GRAS alone is not enough).
Inhalable ingredient suppliers approved with an inhalation-grade statement.
Ingestible products are protected from contamination and every label carries an accurate allergen declaration.
Sticker templates per SKU with an allergen declaration printed on the label.
Topicals are protected from contamination, risk-assessed for skin or mucosal absorption and duration of use, and labeled with fragrance, skin irritant and allergen declarations.
Develop, document and run a HACCP system based on the 12 Codex Alimentarius steps as part of the quality system.
HACCP: plans per product / process built on the 12 Codex steps; only complete, validated plans go active, and CCP checks run against the active version.
A documented multidisciplinary HACCP team (quality, sanitation, maintenance, senior management) with one member and one backup certified in an International HACCP Alliance approved course.

Team members and roles. HACCP certified people (one plus a backup) tracked in Training. HACCP: team members with role and department; one person and a backup certified (certificate on file) before any plan can be validated.

A description for each finished product: name, safety characteristics (water activity, pH, cannabinoids), ingredients, allergens, packaging, intended use, target market, shelf life, labeling instructions, storage and distribution.

SKU specs, formulations, sticker templates (ingredients, instructions, warning). HACCP: product description per plan (name, safety characteristics, ingredients, allergens, packaging, intended use, target market, shelf life, labeling, storage).
A flow diagram for each product and process showing every step, inputs, outsourced steps, rework, waste and by-products, with CCPs marked, reviewed yearly or on change.
Batch Tracker steps per batch type. HACCP: process flow with inputs, steps, outsourced steps, rework, end products and waste, CCPs marked, drawn as a diagram; reviewed yearly through the reanalysis.
A hazard analysis matching the flow diagram that covers every product, material and packaging, and records each biological, chemical and physical hazard, its cause and its control.
HACCP: hazard analysis for every flow step (biological, chemical, physical, allergen) with cause, control measure and significance.
Identify from the hazard analysis the steps that need CCPs, documented so they prevent, remove or reduce each hazard.
HACCP: CCPs set on the flow steps that control significant hazards.
Measurable critical limits for each CCP that separate acceptable from unacceptable product.
HACCP: a measurable critical limit for every CCP.
Documented monitoring that keeps each CCP within its limits.
Batch records capture the process values. HACCP: CCP monitoring records with measured value, within limits or not, verified by a second person.
Specific corrective actions for each CCP that bring it back under control and keep affected product from consumers.
Out-of-control CCPs handled as deviations and CAPAs. HACCP: a CCP out of limits needs the corrective action and the product disposition; a deviation can be raised from it.
Validate control measures and critical limits before use and again after significant product or process changes.

HACCP: validation evidence required before a plan is activated; revising a plan clears the validation. Change control: a change that affects HACCP cannot be implemented until the plan is reviewed and revalidated.
Ongoing verification that HACCP is followed and works, with a full reanalysis yearly or after significant change.

HACCP: verification records (records review, calibration, yearly reanalysis) with findings; reanalysis due date per plan. Change control: changes affecting HACCP trigger the plan review. Verification schedule dates HACCP verification and CCP record review.
Quality system personnel and org chart
An organizational chart showing reporting lines and everyone involved in safety, quality and CSQ conformance, with their functions and responsibilities.

Team members with roles. Org chart: positions with reporting lines, the person and backup, functions and responsibilities, and who holds each safety / quality / CSQ role (senior management, quality lead and backup flagged when missing).
Quality policies and measurable objectives suited to the business, with a process to change, review and keep improving them.
Quality objectives: measurable targets with owners, counted from Hendrix records where possible; targets changed or dropped only with a recorded reason.

Senior management reviews the system at least yearly: previous actions, complaints and feedback, internal, external and regulatory audits, risks and corrective actions, resources, CSQ conformance, and changes; minutes kept and shared.

Management review: every input (previous actions, complaints, audits, CAPAs, risks, HACCP, KPIs, CSQ conformance, changes, suppliers, verification, resources) filled from Hendrix records and discussed; signed by Full access, next review within 12 months, actions tracked, minutes shared.
Measurable improvement goals with KPIs and effectiveness checks, continuing education per role, shared with staff and reviewed at least quarterly.
Continued education per role in the training matrix. KPIs measured every month or quarter; a missed target needs the action taken; KPI board printed to share with staff.

A change management plan for people, processes and products: what each change affects, how it is documented and approved, training before use, and who is told (including regulators and the certification body).

Audit trail records every change with a reason. Change control: impact assessment, approval by Full access, actions, training before use, notifications (regulator, certification body, customers) and an effectiveness check; approved changes cannot be rewritten.
Risk procedures: the hazard, its root cause, the owner, immediate action, timescale for a permanent fix, verification, and routine surveillance of product safety and quality.

Risk register: each risk with the hazard, root cause, owner, rating (likelihood x severity), immediate action and target date for the permanent fix; controlled only with verification; routine review on a schedule with every review kept.

Validate facilities and equipment with installation, operational and performance qualification (IQ, OQ, PQ), materials through supplier approval, and revalidate yearly and whenever critical limits, cGMPs or CSQ conformance change.
Materials validated through supplier approval. Equipment register: IQ, OQ and PQ recorded per piece of equipment with yearly revalidation.
Verification procedures that list the activities to verify, who does them, how often, and how they are monitored and recorded.

Verification schedule: each activity with how, who, how often and where it is recorded; last dates taken from Hendrix records (sanitation, CCP, HACCP, calibration, audits, tests, risks, KPIs, management review, suppliers) or recorded here; overdue flagged.
Everyone acknowledges the safety and quality commitments, training covers anyone who affects product, improvements are planned and measured, and the culture policy is reviewed yearly.
Quality policy as an SOP; every signature recorded per version. Training per person in the training matrix.
Know and meet customer requirements, have a channel for product information, feedback and complaints, and measure whether customers are satisfied.
Customer feedback logged with a satisfaction rating; complaints and feedback tracked per customer.
New products and changes are approved by a qualified person, trial runs prove the process when needed, and every product has a full process description and flow diagram kept current.
A SKU cannot be switched on without a formulation. Change control: new products and changes approved by a qualified person; a trial run must pass before use when required.

Process specs with limits for every critical parameter, and product specs covering name and form, physical and chemical traits, contaminants, storage, shelf life, serving size, cannabinoid and terpene content, allergens, ingredients, reagents, packaging and devices, excise stamps and label, and customer and legal requirements.
SKU specs, formulations, sticker servings and weight.
Product and process verification and validation
Verify and validate that products and processes meet spec, with at least three consecutive batches meeting spec unless otherwise required.
Batch and test records per SKU.
